title: Declarative Terraform state-machine for Private EKS control plane provisioning
creator: Maya Rodriguez
description: Build a declarative Terraform-based state-machine module that manages lifecycle for Redwood Private (VPC) EKS control plane provisioning. The module should encode idempotent steps (network preflight, cluster creation, node bootstrap hooks, KMS/certs integration, post-provision healthchecks) and expose clear state transitions, retry/backoff semantics and safe rollback/cleanup paths. This is intended to replace fragile ad-hoc scripts currently used by infra-oncall and provide deterministic upgrade/rollback behavior for private control planes deployed through Redwood Private. The module must integrate with existing Redwood IaC patterns, emit tracing-friendly state events to the platform's observability pipeline, and provide outputs that enable higher-level orchestration (console rollouts, canary controllers).
acceptance_criteria: Module is published in our terraform registry namespace and has semver tagging
Provisioning run is idempotent: repeated apply on same config results in no-op or safe reconciliation
Explicit state transitions logged for each step (preflight -> create -> post-checks -> ready) and visible in observability dashboard via events link
Automatic, configurable retry/backoff on transient failures with documented max attempts
Safe rollback: on a terminal failure the module reverts network/KMS changes or marks cluster for safe teardown with a remediation checklist
Healthcheck hooks (API server readiness, cert rotation check, node control-plane reachability, kube-apiserver TLS sanity) executed and failures surfaced as diagnostic messages
Module integrates with existing KMS key rotation and cross-account IAM roles without requiring manual intervention
Comprehensive unit and integration tests (terraform-validator checks + small E2E dry-run in staging) are added
Documented example usage for a VPC with private subnet topology and external KMS, and migration notes for teams currently using the older provisioner script
design_decisions: Use a declarative state-file pattern in Terraform with a small 'controller' Lambda step (kept optional) to coordinate long-running transitions rather than imperative scripts
Model control-plane lifecycle as named states to simplify observability and make rollbacks deterministic
Keep costly cloud operations (create cluster, create kms alias) idempotent and wrapped with safe preflight checks
Avoid operator SDK dependency for initial rollout — module should be usable by customers who only consume Terraform
Emit lightweight SNS/S3 state events so platform observability can consume them without coupling to implementation
Expose hooks for post-provision automation (e.g., bootstrap config, node pool attachment) but do not bake heavy business logic into module
implementation_notes: Split the repo into module/ (terraform resources) and scripts/ (small orchestration helpers). Keep the Lambda controller code under scripts/lambdas with acceptance tests.
Preflight tasks: validate VPC subnets, NAT/route table config, IAM principal trust, KMS key policy, DNS delegation
Create a lightweight state S3 object keyed by control-plane id and terraform workspace to persist step progress (encrypted with KMS)
Backoff policy: exponential starting at 10s up to 10m, max attempts configurable default 5
Healthchecks: implement modular checks so teams can opt-in/out; failures produce structured logs with remediation hints
Testing: use terraform-compliance + kitchen-terraform for unit/integration; add a staged E2E where cluster creation is a dry-run and healthchecks mocked
Provide migration helper scripts to read older provisioner artifacts and bring them into the new state model
Make observability hooks idempotent and attach a run_id to each apply; ensure run_id surfaces in console traces and cost dashboards
risks: Long-running cloud operations could exceed Terraform apply timeouts — mitigated by offloading coordination to optional controller Lambda
Accidental teardown risk if state mapping between old provisioner and new module is incorrect — mitigation: migration tool + dry-run mode
KMS and cross-account IAM changes pose security risk during automated rollback — require guardrails and manual approval gates for destructive paths
Increased surface area for post-provision hooks could hide platform-specific logic inside module — mitigate by keeping hooks opt-in and documented
